Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: Sternpost rudder: a Han pottery boat model (1st century CE) from Guangzhou, and European depictions c. 1180; lateen sail: Mediterranean, 2nd century CE iconography, excavated rigs from about 400 CE. Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: Panemone (vertical-axis) windmills reported from Persia, dated between the 7th and 10th centuries by different authors; horizontal-axis post mills in north-west Europe from the 1180s (earliest certain English reference 1185, Weedley, Yorkshire). Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: Disputed: William Clement (London, turret clock for King's College, Cambridge, 1671) is the traditional attribution; Joseph Knibb supplied an anchor-escapement turret clock for Wadham College, Oxford in 1670; Robert Hooke's claim rests on a statement of William Derham (1696) and has no documentary support. Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: Christiaan Huygens (spiral spring watch, announced in the Journal des Sçavans, February 1675) and Robert Hooke (claimed since 1658–1660s; a spring-regulated watch was shown in 1675); Isaac Thuret made watches for Huygens; the priority dispute was not settled in England. Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: Posed by the voyages of the 15th–17th centuries; the Longitude Act of 1714 (Queen Anne) offered up to £20,000 for a method accurate to half a degree at the end of a voyage to the West Indies (lesser prizes for 1° and 2/3°); the clock approach was proposed by Gemma Frisius in 1530, the lunar-distance method by others. Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: John Harrison, H1 (1735), H2, H3, then the watch-form H4 (completed 1759); H4 was tested on a voyage to Jamaica (1761–62) and to Barbados (1764) and its timekeeping met the terms of the Longitude Act; the Board of Longitude paid Harrison in stages (the full award was long delayed). Reported performance: about 5 seconds slow after 81 days to Jamaica (figure disputed, see the text). Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: John Hadley (octant, 1731) and, independently, Thomas Godfrey of Philadelphia (about 1730–31); Isaac Newton described a similar instrument to Halley earlier, but his description was published only after Halley's death in 1742; the sextant (a 60° arc) followed in the 1750s. Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: Oldest surviving example: the alabaster outflow clepsydra from Karnak, in the reign of Amenhotep III (14th century BCE); a tomb inscription of the official Amenemhet (16th century BCE) is the oldest record of one; Ctesibius of Alexandria (3rd century BCE) is credited with the constant-head overflow. Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: Origin disputed: stereographic projection is attributed to Hipparchus (2nd century BCE) and treated by Ptolemy (Planisphaerium); the oldest surviving treatise is by John Philoponus (about 550 CE), the first astrolabes in the Islamic world are credited to al-Fazari (8th century), and the earliest surviving instrument is dated 927–928 CE. Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: Shen Kuo, Dream Pool Essays (1088): magnetised needle and magnetic declination; Zhu Yu, Pingzhou Ketan (written about 1111–1117): use at sea; Alexander Neckam in Europe (about 1187–1190). Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: Anonymous, probably in northern Italy or England, late 13th century: the earliest tower clocks are recorded from about 1283–1300 (Dunstable, Westminster, Canterbury) and the first clear drawing of an escapement is in the Dondi manuscript (1364); the Salisbury Cathedral clock (about 1386) is an early surviving example whose original escapement is uncertain. Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: The spring-driven clock appears in the early 15th century; the oldest surviving fusee clock is a table clock made for Philip the Good of Burgundy, dated by its decoration to about 1430–1435 (a fusee also appears in a crossbow in a manuscript of 1405 and in drawings of Brunelleschi and Leonardo); the common attribution of the fusee to Jacob Zech of Prague (about 1525) is wrong.
